newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign names in India's anniversary irk critics.
newsitem.headline: Foreign names in India's anniversary irk critics.

text.p: The high-profile presence of foreign brandnames in the celebration of India's 50th anniversary of independence has irked critics, who say the names tarnish the objectives of the freedom struggle.

Cola-maker PepsiCo International, toothpaste firm Colgate-Palmolive India and Viacom-owned Music Television (MTV) are grabbing television viewers with sponsorships and advertisements marking India's freedom.
Critics consider the multinational names as symbols of foreign economic domination or western culture.

"It is a total reversal of the value system and the very inspiration which led us in the struggle. We are back to square one," socialist economist S.K.Goyal, an adviser to former prime minister Chandra Shekhar, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Much before India's officials kicked off the completion of the golden jubilee on August 15, millions of fans watched the Independence Cup, a four-nation cricket tournament in May sponsored by cola-maker Pepsi.
Critics see Pepsi as an undesirable symbol of India's open door economic policies that started in 1991.
Music Television (MTV), has run into criticism after marking the channel's logo in saffron, white and green, the colours of India's national flag.

"Celebrating India's independence is a good thing. But capitalising on this is bad. This has to stop immediately," the Statesman quoted Deepika Chikhalia, a lawmaker for the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) as saying.
"Imagine watching a Samantha Fox number with the tricolour on top of it," she said.
MTV's press officer was quoted as saying: "At least we are not boring the audience by giving them an overdose of Indian-ness."

An angry letter to the editor of the Times of India moaned about India's poverty and the poor living conditions of rural citizens and raised questions on independence programmes being made by the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

"We are celebrating 50 years of Independence but the tragedy is that the nation must relive the magic of the drama through a BBC television series on India's Independence," Deepak Mukarji said in the letter published on Wednesday.
"Is the world's largest film industry (in Bombay) too incompetent to produce a similar series on India?" he asked.
